title: Redis Sentinel for High Availability
description: Learn how Redis Sentinel provides automatic failover and monitoring for a single master-replica Redis deployment.

data.text: Redis Sentinel is a distributed system that monitors Redis master and replica instances, automatically promoting a replica to master when the current master fails. Unlike Redis Cluster, Sentinel does not shard data — it provides high availability for a single dataset across multiple nodes.

A Sentinel deployment requires at least 3 instances to avoid split-brain issues. Sentinels communicate using a gossip protocol to agree on the current master's status. When a quorum (majority) of Sentinels detects that the master is unreachable, they collectively promote one of the replicas. This quorum-based approach ensures only one master exists at any time.

data.title: The 3-Node Rule
data.text: Always run an odd number of Sentinel instances (3 or 5 is recommended). With only 2 Sentinels, a network partition can cause both to disagree, leaving the cluster without a valid master.

data.text: Clients connect to Sentinel rather than directly to the master. When they need the current master address, they query Sentinel using the command SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name. If the master changes, Sentinel notifies connected clients, which then reconnect to the new master.

data.title: Redis Sentinel Configuration (redis-sentinel.conf)
data.code:
port 26379

dir /tmp

# Monitor the master named 'mymaster'
sentinel monitor mymaster redis-master 6379 2

# Replica authentication
sentinel auth-pass mymaster MySecurePassword

# Require 2 seconds of unresponsiveness before declaring failure
sentinel down-after-milliseconds mymaster 5000

# 5 second failover timeout
sentinel failover-timeout mymaster 5000

# Parallel syncs during failover
sentinel parallel-syncs mymaster 1

terms.definition: The minimum number of Sentinels that must agree before a decision (like failover) is executed.
Subjective Down — when a single Sentinel determines a node is unreachable.
Objective Down — when enough Sentinels agree a node is down to trigger a failover.

items.question: How does Sentinel differ from Redis Cluster?
items.answer: Sentinel provides high availability for a single dataset without sharding. Redis Cluster shards data across multiple masters and provides both scaling and high availability.

items.question: What happens during a network partition?
items.answer: The partition with the quorum majority of Sentinels performs failover. The minority partition cannot elect a new master and its clients become read-only or disconnected.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use 3 or 5 Sentinel instances for reliable quorum-based failover
Clients connect to Sentinel, not directly to the master
Sentinel does not shard data — it protects a single dataset
Failover happens automatically within seconds of detecting the master is down
data.takeaway: Redis Sentinel is the simplest way to add high availability to Redis, making it ideal when you need failover but not data sharding.
